etymology: Hebrew Tsela, “rib” or “side”; a town in the tribe of Benjamin, the burial-place of Saul and Jonathan in the sepulchre of Kish.
biblical_def: Zela (Zelah) was a town in the lot of Benjamin, listed among its cities: “And Zelah, Eleph, and Jebusi, which is Jerusalem, Gibeath, and Kirjath; fourteen cities with their villages” (Josh 18:28). Its chief memory is a solemn one, for it held the family sepulchre of Kish, and there David laid to rest the bones of Saul and Jonathan when they were brought back from the men of Jabesh-gilead: “And the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son buried they in the country of Benjamin in Zelah, in the sepulchre of Kish his father: and they performed all that the king commanded. And after that God was intreated for the land” (2Sa 21:14). Here the fallen king of Israel came home at last to his father’s grave, and the long famine was ended when honour was done to the dead and justice satisfied for the blood of the Gibeonites. Zela preaches the sober dignity of burial and the mercy of God that answers when His people set right what was wrong. Even Saul, who died in his sin, was given an honourable grave among his fathers; and the God who was intreated for the land is the God who buries His saints in hope of a better resurrection.
webster_summary: A town of Benjamin holding the sepulchre of Kish, where Saul and Jonathan were buried (Josh 18:28; 2Sa 21:14); a witness to the dignity of burial and the mercy of God intreated for the land.

etymology: Hebrew ha-Eleph, “the ox” or “the thousand” (read in the KJV as Eleph); a town in the tribe of Benjamin, named once.
biblical_def: Haeleph, read in the Authorized Version simply as Eleph, was a town in the lot of Benjamin, named beside Zela: “And Zelah, Eleph, and Jebusi, which is Jerusalem, Gibeath, and Kirjath; fourteen cities with their villages” (Josh 18:28). The name means “the ox” or, by another reading, “the thousand,” the unit into which the tribes were mustered for war and reckoning. Both senses fit a working town of Benjamin: the ox that plowed the field and trod out the corn, and the thousand that marched under its captain. This obscure town stood within the same small tribal portion that held Jerusalem itself, the city of the great King. Benjamin was the least of the tribes and its lot the smallest, yet Moses blessed it, “The beloved of the LORD shall dwell in safety by him; and the LORD shall cover him all the day long, and he shall dwell between his shoulders” (Deu 33:12). Haeleph, a plowman’s town in the beloved little tribe, preaches that greatness with God is not measured by size. The ox labours unseen, the thousand marches unnamed, and the least tribe holds the holy city; for the LORD delights to put His treasure in small and humble vessels.

etymology: Hebrew Avvim, “ruins” or “the Avvites”; a town in the tribe of Benjamin, named once; the name recalls the ancient Avvites, an early people of the land.
biblical_def: Avim was a town in the lot of Benjamin, listed once: “And Avim, and Parah, and Ophrah” (Josh 18:23). The name recalls the Avvim, an ancient people who once dwelt in the land in the hamlets as far as Gaza before the Caphtorim destroyed them and dwelt in their stead. That a town in Benjamin should bear the name of a people long swept away is a quiet memorial of the passing of the nations. The land of promise had known many peoples before Israel — Avvim, Anakim, Rephaim, Emim, Horites — each in turn dispossessed, until the LORD gave the land to the seed of Abraham according to His oath. Avim, an old name in a Benjamite field, preaches the sovereignty of God over the rise and fall of peoples. He removeth kings and setteth up kings; He gave the Avvim their little day and then their end; He planted Israel where they had been. The believer, seeing the ruins of the mighty and the graves of the forgotten, learns to fear the God who holds all nations in His hand as the small dust of the balance, and to build his hope on the kingdom that cannot be moved.

etymology: Hebrew Kephar ha-Ammoni, “the village of the Ammonite”; a town in the tribe of Benjamin, named once.
biblical_def: Chephar-haammonai, “the village of the Ammonite,” was a town in the lot of Benjamin, named once: “And Chepharhaammonai, and Ophni, and Gaba; twelve cities with their villages” (Josh 18:24). Its name, marking it a village of Ammonites, is a curious survival within Israel’s borders, perhaps a settlement of that people, or a place taking its name from some old dealing with them. The Ammonites were kin to Israel, descended from Lot, yet they were a snare and an enemy through much of her history, and no Ammonite was to enter the congregation of the LORD to the tenth generation. That a Benjamite town should be called the village of the Ammonite is a reminder that the people of God dwelt always in the near neighbourhood of the nations, hemmed about by kindred who were also foes. The town preaches the danger of unequal fellowship and the call to separation. Israel was to be a peculiar people, not mingling with the surrounding nations nor learning their ways; yet grace could reach even an Ammonite, as it reached Ruth the Moabitess and Naaman the Syrian. Chephar-haammonai stands on the border of that tension: separation from the world’s idolatry, yet mercy held out to any who would come and take hold of the covenant.

etymology: Hebrew Ophrah, “fawn” or “dust”; a town in the tribe of Benjamin, named once; distinct from Ophrah of the Abiezrites, the home of Gideon in Manasseh.
biblical_def: Ophrah was a town in the lot of Benjamin, named once with Avim and Parah: “And Avim, and Parah, and Ophrah” (Josh 18:23). It is to be distinguished from the more famous Ophrah of the Abiezrites in Manasseh, the home of Gideon, where the angel of the LORD sat under the oak and where Gideon threshed wheat and afterward set up the ephod that became a snare. This Benjamite Ophrah has no such story; it is a name in the roll of the tribe’s inheritance and no more. Its name, “fawn,” is gentle and fitting for a quiet hill-town of Benjamin, the beloved little tribe of whom Moses said, “The beloved of the LORD shall dwell in safety by him” (Deu 33:12). The obscurity of this Ophrah, overshadowed by its famous namesake, preaches contentment in a hidden place. Not every town can be a Gideon’s Ophrah, remembered for great deeds; most are like this one, known only to God and their own people. Yet the beloved of the LORD dwelt there in safety under His covering, and that is portion enough for any place or any soul that rests beneath the shadow of the Almighty.

etymology: Hebrew Gittayim, “two winepresses”; a town of Benjamin to which the men of Beeroth fled and sojourned; reinhabited after the exile.
biblical_def: Gittaim, “two winepresses,” was a town associated with Benjamin, remembered as the refuge of the Beerothites: “And the Beerothites fled to Gittaim, and were sojourners there until this day” (2Sa 4:3). Beeroth was one of the cities of the Gibeonites, reckoned to Benjamin, and for some cause its people fled and became sojourners — resident strangers — in Gittaim. After the Babylonian exile the town was inhabited again, for the children of Benjamin dwelt at Gittaim among other places (Neh 11:33). The name, “two winepresses,” speaks of a place of vintage, where the grapes were trodden and the wine ran out. Yet its history is a history of displacement: a people driven from their home, dwelling as strangers in another’s town for generations. Gittaim preaches the pilgrim condition of the people of God, who are strangers and sojourners on the earth, confessing that here they have no continuing city but seek one to come. As the Beerothites sojourned in Gittaim, so the saints sojourn in this world, treading through the winepress of affliction toward the city whose builder and maker is God, where the tears of exile are wiped away for ever.

etymology: Hebrew Ananyah, “the LORD hath covered” or “whom the LORD answers”; a town of Benjamin reinhabited after the exile, named once.
biblical_def: Ananiah was a town of Benjamin, listed among the villages resettled by the returning exiles: “And at Anathoth, Nob, Ananiah” (Neh 11:32). Its name is a confession, “the LORD hath covered” or “whom the LORD answers,” carrying the divine name and a testimony of covering and answered prayer. That such a town was rebuilt and reinhabited after the desolation of the captivity is itself a mercy: the returning remnant, few and feeble, took up their dwelling again in the old places, and the very name of the town preached the faithfulness that had brought them home. The LORD had covered His people through the long night of exile and answered the prayers of Daniel and the fathers, restoring them to the land. Ananiah stands among the resettled towns as a monument to that covering grace. It reminds the church in every age that God does not cast off His people for ever; though He chasten them and scatter them, He remembers His covenant, covers their nakedness, answers their cry, and gathers them again. The town whose name means “the LORD hath covered” is a small perpetual witness to the God who restores.

etymology: Hebrew Chatsor, “enclosure” or “village”; a town of Benjamin reinhabited after the exile; distinct from the great Hazor of Naphtali burned by Joshua.
biblical_def: This Hazor was a town of Benjamin, named among the places resettled by the returning exiles: “Hazor, Ramah, Gittaim” (Neh 11:33). It must be distinguished from the great Hazor of the north, the royal city of Jabin in Naphtali which Joshua burned, and from other towns of the same common name; the word simply means an enclosure or walled village, and many places bore it. This Benjamite Hazor is remembered only as one of the villages where the remnant dwelt again after the captivity, near Ramah and Gittaim. Its very commonness is instructive: a plain name for a plain place, one enclosure among many, holding a handful of returned families. The resettlement of these obscure towns was the quiet work by which God restored His people after judgment — not with trumpets, but village by village, household by household, the land was peopled again. Hazor of Benjamin preaches that the great works of God are often done in small and ordinary ways. The kingdom comes not always with observation; it is built up in hidden places, in unremarked towns and unremembered families, until the whole is gathered and the purpose of God stands complete.

etymology: Hebrew Reqem, “variegated” or “embroidery”; a town in the tribe of Benjamin, named once; distinct from the men of the same name.
biblical_def: Rekem was a town in the lot of Benjamin, named once with Irpeel and Taralah: “And Rekem, and Irpeel, and Taralah” (Josh 18:27). This is a place, not to be confused with Rekem the Midianite prince slain in the war of vengeance, nor with the man Rekem of the line of Judah. The name suggests something “variegated” or embroidered, many-coloured, and though nothing of the town’s story survives, the name itself is a small delight, hinting at variety and adornment. It joins the roll of Benjamin’s cities, each a distinct thread in the woven inheritance of the tribe. The variety of the towns preaches the manifold wisdom of God, who made no two places, no two men, no two saints alike, but delights in a rich diversity within the unity of His people. As a garment of many colours was the token of a father’s special love to Joseph, so the varied towns of the tribes, and the varied gifts and graces of the church, are the embroidery of God’s workmanship. Rekem, a many-coloured name in Benjamin, reminds us that the body of Christ is one, yet its members many and diverse, each set in the place that pleased the great Designer.

etymology: Hebrew Alemeth, “covering” or “hiding-place” (also called Almon); a Levitical city in the tribe of Benjamin, given to the priests, the sons of Aaron.
biblical_def: Alemeth, also called Almon, was a Levitical city in the tribe of Benjamin, one of the towns given out of the tribes to the priests, the sons of Aaron: “And out of the tribe of Benjamin; Geba with her suburbs, and Alemeth with her suburbs, and Anathoth with her suburbs” (1Ch 6:60); and under the name Almon in the earlier list, “Anathoth with her suburbs, and Almon with her suburbs; four cities” (Josh 21:18). The Levites received no continuous territory of their own, for the LORD was their inheritance; instead they were scattered through the tribes in these cities, that the worship, the law, and the priesthood might be spread among all the people. Alemeth, whose name means “covering” or “hiding-place,” was one such priestly town near Anathoth, the home of Jeremiah. It preaches the wisdom of God in scattering His ministers among the people, so that no tribe was left without the light of the law near at hand. And its name, a hiding-place, points to the LORD Himself, who is the true covering of His priests and people: “Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble.” The Levite who had no land of his own found his portion and his shelter in God alone.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A priestly town raises no modern quarrel. Its name, “hiding-place,” and its office as a Levitical city simply preach the portion of the priests: not land, but the LORD.

The principle to recover is that the LORD is the inheritance and covering of His ministers. The Levites received no continuous territory, but were scattered in cities through the tribes, that the law and worship might be near all the people; for God Himself was their portion. And His name is their shelter: “Thou art my hiding place.” The minister of Christ still finds his treasure not in earthly possession but in the God he serves.
